extracted.intended_audience: patent litigators, appellate counsel, patent practitioners, and judges handling §145 actions and prosecution-laches disputes
extracted.subtask_description: Legal standards and appellate-review rules governing prosecution laches defenses, Article III jurisdiction, and related procedural doctrines in appeals from district-court §145 actions and PTAB decisions. Focuses on what must be proved, how courts review those findings, and jurisdictional limits for pending claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard_of_review_for_district_court_findings
rubrics_metrics.description: We review a district court’s conclusions of law de novo and its factual findings for clear error; we review a district court’s determination of prosecution laches for abuse of discretion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Citations and thresholds: Endo Pharms. Sols., Inc. v. Custopharm Inc., 894 F.3d 1374, 1379 (Fed. Cir. 2018) (law de novo; facts for clear error). Prosecution-laches determinations are reviewed for abuse of discretion (Hyatt I, 998 F.3d at 1359). An abuse of discretion can be shown when the court 'exercised its discretion based upon an error of law or clearly erroneous factual findings.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Availability_of_prosecution_laches_in_§145_actions
rubrics_metrics.description: The PTO can assert the defense of prosecution laches in a §145 action; that question was resolved in Hyatt I and is law of the case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The opinion states: 'We hold that it can' (Hyatt I, 998 F.3d at 1362). Arguments re-litigating whether prosecution laches survives the Patent Act or applies to §145 were foreclosed by law-of-the-case because they were considered and rejected in prior appeal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elements_of_prosecution_laches
rubrics_metrics.description: Prosecution laches requires showing an unreasonable and unexplainable delay in prosecution and that the delay was prejudicial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Like in infringement actions, the party asserting prosecution laches 'must show the delay was prejudicial.' (Hyatt I, 998 F.3d at 1369–71). The defense involves both a showing of inexcusable delay and prejudice to the patentee or public interests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden_of_proof_on_prosecution_laches_defendant
rubrics_metrics.description: The party asserting prosecution laches (here, the PTO) bears the burden of proving that the applicant engaged in unreasonable/unexplained delay and that the delay was prejudicial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hyatt I remanded to permit presentation of evidence on prejudice; the PTO must satisfy its burden, and the district court's findings on whether the burden was met are reviewed for abuse of discretion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Law_of_the_case_doctrine_application
rubrics_metrics.description: When a court decides a rule of law, that decision should continue to govern the same issues in subsequent stages of the same case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Issues decided 'explicitly or by necessary inference from the disposition' constitute law of the case (ArcelorMittal France v. AK Steel Corp., 786 F.3d 885, 888; Kori Corp. v. Wilco Marsh Buggies & Draglines, Inc., 761 F.2d 649, 657). The doctrine precludes relitigation of issues already decided on prior appeal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forfeiture_of_arguments_not_made_below
rubrics_metrics.description: An appellant forfeits arguments not presented to the district court and therefore cannot raise them on appeal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited authority: Ironburg Inventions Ltd. v. Valve Corp., 64 F.4th 1274, 1286 (Fed. Cir. 2023); In re Google Tech. Holdings LLC, 980 F.3d 858, 863 (Fed. Cir. 2020). The opinion notes Mr. Hyatt failed to develop a particular justification before the district court, so the argument is forfeited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Article_III_standing_requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: To invoke federal-court power a party must allege an actual case or controversy and demonstrate standing by showing (1) injury in fact, (2) traceability to the challenged conduct, and (3) redressability by a favorable decision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Citations: O'Shea v. Littleton, Lujan v. Defs. of Wildlife, Wittman v. Personhuballah. The need to satisfy these requirements 'persists throughout the life of the lawsuit.' A party may rely on statutory rights to confer standing but still must satisfy Article III's constitutional requirements (Spokeo).

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence_requirement_when_jurisdiction_disputed_later
rubrics_metrics.description: When jurisdiction is disputed during later phases of litigation, the party invoking federal jurisdiction must show injury by submitting affidavits or other evidence; a bare pleading is insufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wittman, 578 U.S. at 545: 'The party invoking federal jurisdiction must show he suffered an injury by submitting 'affidavit[s] or other evidence.' The opinion assumes a bare allegation of dissatisfaction may suffice at the pleading stage but not through later litigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope_of_§145_statutory_remedy_and_Article_III_limits
rubrics_metrics.description: §145 provides that an 'applicant dissatisfied with the decision of the [Board]' may bring a civil action in district court and the court 'may adjudge that such applicant is entitled to receive a patent for his invention, as specified in any of his claims involved in the decision of the [Board]'.  But §145 does not override Article III: the applicant must still satisfy Article III's standing requirements as to each pending claim submitted to the district court.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The court rejects treating the Board's decision as an 'undivided whole' to bypass Article III. Congress can create statutory rights but cannot erase constitutional standing requirements (Spokeo). Thus §145 confers a statutory remedy but does not automatically confer Article III jurisdiction over claims where no injury is shown.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sufficiency_of_dissatisfaction_allegation_at_pleading_stage
rubrics_metrics.description: A bare allegation of dissatisfaction with the Board's decision may be assumed sufficient to establish Article III jurisdiction at the pleading stage, but that allegation must be supported by evidence later in the litigation when jurisdiction is contested.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The court states: 'We assume, without deciding, that Mr. Hyatt’s bare allegation of dissatisfaction with the Board’s decision is enough to establish Article III jurisdiction over the Board’s reversal of the examiner’s rejections at the pleading stage.' But later, the party must produce evidence of injury (see Wittman).

rubrics_metrics.name: No_automatic_entitlement_to_patent_after_board_reversal
rubrics_metrics.description: A Board reversal of an examiner’s rejection does not necessarily require the PTO to issue a patent immediately; prosecution may continue until the PTO is satisfied that an 'applicant is entitled to a patent under the law.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statutory reference: 35 U.S.C. § 151(a) and case law (BlackLight Power, Inc. v. Rogan, 295 F.3d 1269, 1273–74). The opinion explains that Mr. Hyatt's theory that the PTO's 'failure to issue them' (the patents) is an injury is false because reversal does not mandate immediate issuance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mootness_of_other_issues_when_laches_disposes_case
rubrics_metrics.description: If a district court's judgment for the PTO on prosecution laches is affirmed, it can render moot other pending appeals (e.g., anticipation and written-description issues).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The opinion notes that because laches was adjudicated in PTO's favor, the PTO's pending appeals on anticipation and written-description are now moot (citing eSimplicity, Inc. v. United States).

rubrics_metrics.name: Weight_of_trial_record_and_deference_to_district_court_factfinding
rubrics_metrics.description: A district court's thorough trial record — hundreds of exhibits admitted, lengthy post-trial briefs, numerous factual findings — supports deference on appeal absent clear error or abuse of discretion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: district court made 247 findings of fact after a nearly three-week bench trial and over 1,000 pages of post-trial briefing. The appellate court will not find abuse of discretion where the district court weighed evidence and made findings that were not challenged on appeal.
